corrected_payload.answer: No. The algebraic argument is a valid proof by contradiction, but its claimed conclusion has the direction reversed. Assuming sqrt(2)=a/b in lowest terms gives a^2=2b^2. Since an even square has an even base, a is even; writing a=2k then gives b^2=2k^2, so b is even as well. Thus 2 divides both a and b, contradicting lowest terms. Consequently no lowest-terms integer quotient can equal sqrt(2), and sqrt(2) is irrational (using the standard fact that a rational number has such a representation).

proof_steps.justification: From a^2=2b^2, a^2 is even. If a were odd, a=2r+1 for some integer r, so a^2=4r(r+1)+1 would be odd. Hence a is even.
Write a=2k. Substitution into a^2=2b^2 gives 4k^2=2b^2, hence b^2=2k^2. The same odd-square argument used in derive-even-numerator shows that b is even.
The preceding steps give 2|a and 2|b. Thus a and b have the common divisor 2, contrary to the scoped lowest-terms assumption.
